html:
The Mahabharata is one of the two great Sanskrit epics of India and the longest poem in the world, at about 100,000 verses. It grew over centuries, roughly from 400 BCE to 400 CE, and no single author wrote it, though tradition names the sage Vyasa.

It tells of a war for the throne of the Kuru kingdom between two sets of cousins, the five Pandava brothers and the hundred Kauravas. The war ends in an eighteen-day battle at Kurukshetra, north of Delhi, that kills almost everyone on both sides.

Around that story the poem gathers law, myth, statecraft and philosophy. It says of itself that what is not found here is found nowhere. Its best known part is the Bhagavad Gita, the talk between the warrior Arjuna and Krishna before the battle.

The epic is the work of the centuries after the Vedic period, and with the Ramayana it shaped Hindu belief more than any other text. It spread to Java, Bali and Cambodia, where it is still played in shadow theatre. A 1988 television version emptied Indian streets every Sunday morning.
